scenes.tts: In HeLa cells, the inside of a mitochondrion measured close to P H eight. The Golgi measured close to P H six point six. In mammalian cells, the lysosome sits at P H four point five to five. All three share one cytosol. So how does one cell keep them apart?

scenes.tts: P H is a logarithm, so a small gap hides a large difference. Take the two HeLa averages. The Golgi reads six point five eight. The mitochondrial matrix is estimated at seven point nine eight. They differ by one point four. Ten to the power one point four is about twenty-five. So the Golgi has about twenty-five times the free proton activity of the matrix.

scenes.tts: Think of a room with its own thermostat. The wall does not make the room warm. It slows the loss of heat, so a heater can hold the set point. A cell works the same way. The pump is the heater. Leak is the lost heat. Every difference is a steady state. It lasts only while the pump keeps paying, usually in A T P. Stop the pump, and the difference runs down.

scenes.tts: For protons, the pump is the V A T Pase. It spends A T P to move protons from the cytosol into a lumen. In HeLa cells, a drug called bafilomycin blocks it. Then the Golgi became less acid. So the acidity of the Golgi is not simply there. It is actively kept.

scenes.tts: Calcium follows the same rule. The pump SERCA moves calcium from the cytosol into the E R. The E R lumen holds about half to one millimolar free calcium. The cytosol holds about one hundred nanomolar. That is a five thousand to ten thousand fold difference. Block SERCA with thapsigargin, and calcium leaks out faster than it is replaced.

scenes.tts: Not every compartment is acid. The E R is near neutral, and the mitochondrial matrix is alkaline. Each lumen settles at its own value. That value is a steady state between pumping and leak. It is not set once. A luminal difference lasts only while a pump keeps paying.
